summary: 1935 CCC lookout in Croatan National Forest, named for WWII airman Furnifold Simmons; 96 ft; standing per a 2017 Forest Service notice.

facts.agency: USDA Forest Service, Croatan National Forest
facts.status_note: Standing per a May 2017 Forest Service notice; no later source found.

access.note: On national forest land, and the 2017 notice describes members of the public visiting the site. Level inferred from that; current climbing rules were not found in any source.

events.note: Built by Civilian Conservation Corps workers from Camp Patterson, per the Forest Service.
Furnifold McLendel Simmons, later the tower's namesake, manned the lookout from 1935.
Simmons left the lookout in 1943 for military service. Later staffing is not recorded in these sources.
Carteret County News-Times, June 11, 1948: the tower is now known as the Simmons tower, and a dedication recently honored him there.
Forest Service notice: the tower is the last of six fire towers still standing on the forest and is eligible for the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.quote: The Newport Fire Tower was built in 1935 by the African American Civilian Conservation Corps Camp Patterson

evidence.supports: Named in honor of Furnifold McLendel Simmons
evidence.quote: later named in honor of fallen World War II veteran, Furnifold McLendel Simmons
Before serving in the war, Simmons manned the lookout from 1935 to 1943.

evidence.supports: Last of six fire towers still standing on the forest; last standing structure built by Camp Patterson
evidence.quote: The tower is the last of six fire towers still standing on the Croatan National Forest and is the last standing structure to have been built by Camp Patterson.

evidence.supports: Eligible for the National Register of Historic Places (not listed)
evidence.quote: It is eligible for the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.supports: Visitors left pet memorials at the site
evidence.quote: There are several remembrances of deceased pets set up at the Newport Simmons Fire Tower by members of the public.

evidence.supports: Private memorials and remains are prohibited on national forest land
evidence.quote: placing private memorials or remains on national forest lands is prohibited.

evidence.supports: Staff to remove remaining monuments on June 15
evidence.quote: Any remaining monuments will be removed by Forest Service staff on June 15 and held at the Croatan Ranger District office for 30 days for owner pick-up.
The 96-foot-tall Newport Tower is the last fire tower standing on the Croatan National Forest.

evidence.supports: Tower one half mile from Newport, now known as the Simmons tower
evidence.quote: The forest observation tower, one half mile from Newport on the Nine Foot road, is now known as the Simmons tower.

evidence.supports: Dedication service in 1948 honored Simmons at the tower
evidence.quote: In special services recently the tower dedicated to the memory of S/Sgt. Furnifold M. Simmons, of Rheims, N.C.

evidence.supports: Simmons was a B-24 crew chief killed in an air crash near Peterson Field on April 5, 1944
evidence.quote: Sergeant Simmons, who was a crew chief of a B-24, was killed in an air crash near Peterson field, Calif., on April 5, 1944.

evidence.supports: Simmons was in Croatan National Forest service August 1935 to February 1943
evidence.quote: From August 1935 to February 1943 Sergeant Simmons was in the Croatan National Forest service.

notes_for_editor: Status and access rest on a May 2017 Forest Service report, so re-check the current condition and climbing rules before publishing a today claim. Height 96 ft comes only from one Flickr caption. The Flickr photo is marked All rights reserved, so it is not added to photos. The brief had no height, status or access; these are new. Two sources give the 1935 start and the 1943 end, and they agree.
